card.title: Potential — work per coulomb, and the electron-volt

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Potential V is work per unit charge (J/C = volt) — a scalar landscape whose slopes push charges: E points downhill, from high V to low. Equipotentials are its contour lines (no work moving along one; field lines cut them at right angles). Potential energy U = qV prices a charge's position. The electron-volt (energy of one e⁻ across 1 V) is atomic-scale currency: 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: V = W/q, 1 V = 1 J/C (MCQ answer)  ·  point charge: V = kQ/r  ·  U = qV  ·  W = n·e·V for n electrons  ·  1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J  ·  gradient: E = −dV/dr (field = steepest descent)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: V = kQ/r takes zero at infinity (isolated charge convention). Equipotential ⟂ field-line geometry needs electrostatics (no induced fields). The eV shortcut applies per elementary charge — multiply by n for n electrons, by 2e for alpha particles.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: One volt is one joule per coulomb — the NEB 2023 1-marker. A charge released from rest runs downhill in V (positive charges) or uphill (electrons). Inside a hollow charged conductor V is constant everywhere (E = 0, no gradient) — electrostatic shielding.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Work moving n electrons across V: each electron gains eV, so W = n·e·V — e.g. 10¹⁸ electrons across 100 V do 10¹⁸ × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 100 = 16 J (NEB 2022, 4-mark pattern). The eV unit skips the powers of ten: the same job is 10²⁰ eV.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Potential is relative — only DIFFERENCES move charges; the zero is a convention (infinity, earth, circuit ground). V = kQ/r fails inside charge distributions (integrate instead). Equipotential reasoning assumes static fields; time-varying fields break the scalar-potential picture.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Bring test charge q₀ from ∞ to r against kQ/r²: W = ∫F·dr = kQq₀/r → V = W/q₀ = kQ/r. Field from potential: a small step dr along E changes V by dV = −E·dr (work done BY the field), so E = −dV/dr — the gradient relation, with the minus encoding 'downhill'.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: '1 volt =' → joule per coulomb, instantly. Energy questions: count charges × e × volts. Equipotential sketches: draw contours, then field lines perpendicular, pointing high→low V.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: NEB 2023 (1): one volt equals 1 joule per coulomb (MCQ). NEB 2022 (4): derive W from V and n flowing electrons. Point-charge V, equipotential properties and gradient relation rotate yearly.
